back: A long, narrow ridge of sand or shingle attached to the land at one end and extending into open water, formed by longshore drift at a change in the direction of the coast.
A ridge of sand or shingle that links an island to the mainland, formed in the wave shadow of the island.
A long ridge of sand or shingle parallel to the coast; a barrier island is separate from the mainland and has a lagoon behind it.
A beach lying parallel to the crests of incoming waves, so that sediment moves up and down the beach with little net movement along it.
A beach lying obliquely to the waves, where longshore drift moves sediment along it; the starting point of a spit.
Sandy beaches are gentle (about 1–5°); shingle beaches are steeper because their permeable sediment gives a weak backwash.

front: Why the end of a spit is recurved
back: Wave refraction and waves from a second direction curve the tip of the spit towards the land.
Storm waves wash sediment from the front to the back of a barrier island, so that it migrates landwards.
Spit: Spurn Head (England; breached in December 2013), Walvis Bay (Namibia). Tombolo: Monte Argentario (Italy). Barrier beach: Chesil Beach (England, about 29 km).
